plan.summary: Bed 3 has Septoria leaf spot, a fungal disease that spreads by splashing water and survives the winter on debris and tomato-related weeds. With the season nearly over and bed 3 already at its season limit for copper sprays, this plan relies on clean-up: remove spotted leaves now, water only by drip, pull weeds, check for new spots through the coming rain, then clear the bed completely and keep tomato-family crops out of it for three years.

steps.title: Remove spotted lower leaves now
steps.detail: On a dry day, cut off every lower leaf and branch with the small dark-edged spots, starting at the west end of the bed, which sits low and dries slowly after rain. Bag the leaves and throw them away rather than composting them. Repeat as new spotted leaves appear. Fungicide is not part of this plan: the spray log shows bed 3 reached its season limit of copper applications in early September, and with the season ending, clean-up does more good.
steps.safety_note: Use only a product registered for this use where you live, and follow its label exactly.

steps.title: Keep the leaves dry: water only by drip
steps.detail: Water bed 3 only through its drip line (zone 2, along the north edge), at the soil, in the morning. Avoid any overhead watering or hosing the leaves, since splashing water carries spores from leaf to leaf. Rain is forecast around 1 November and 4 November, so get the spotted leaves off before then.

steps.title: Pull weeds and volunteer tomatoes around the bed
steps.detail: Pull weeds in and around bed 3, especially tomato-family weeds such as nightshades and ground cherry, and pull up any volunteer tomato seedlings. Septoria survives the winter on some weeds related to tomato.

steps.title: Check for new spots every 3 days
steps.detail: Walk the bed and look for new spots on leaves higher up the plants, on stems and near the fruit, paying most attention to the west end after the forecast rain. Note what you find in #field-reports. If the spots look different from before (rings, greasy patches or spots on the fruit), send a closer, sharper photo of a leaf front and back, or ask your local extension office.

steps.title: Clear out all plants and debris at the end of the season
steps.detail: When you finish picking, pull out all the tomato plants in bed 3, gather as much fallen leaf and plant debris as you can, bag it and throw it away. Take the stakes' ties off and clean them. Work in or till any debris you cannot remove so it breaks down over winter.

steps.title: Plan a 3-year rotation away from bed 3
steps.detail: Plan next year's beds so tomatoes, potatoes, peppers and eggplant don't go back into bed 3 for at least three years. A crop that doesn't get these diseases, such as corn, is a good choice for bed 3. Remember that the peppers in bed 1 are in the same family, so don't simply swap tomatoes into bed 1.

steps.title: Next season: space plants so they don't touch
steps.detail: When you plant tomatoes next season in their new bed, set them far enough apart that grown plants don't touch, so air moves between them and the leaves dry faster after dew or rain. Keep staking on wires and pruning suckers as this year.

steps.title: Next season: mulch around the plants after transplanting
steps.detail: Right after transplanting next season, cover the soil around the tomatoes with an organic mulch such as straw or chopped leaves. It stops spores splashing up from the soil onto the lower leaves.

watch_for: New spots appearing on upper leaves within a week of removing the spotted ones.
Spots spreading quickly along the bed in the five days after the rain forecast around 1 November and 4 November.
Spots appearing on stems or fruit at any point before the bed is cleared.
Spots that look different (rings, greasy patches or fruit lesions) in the next two weeks, which would mean asking for a better photo or the local extension office.
Septoria spots showing up again on next season's tomatoes within the first month after transplanting.

farm_records.title: Bed map
farm_records.text:
Bed map, Maple Row Farm

Six beds run east to west, each 1.2 m wide and 15 m long, with 60 cm paths. Bed 1 is nearest the barn and bed 6 is nearest the fence and the river.

Bed 1: sweet peppers, King of the North. Drip zone 1.
Bed 2: kale, Winterbor. Drip zone 1.
Bed 3: tomatoes, Celebrity, staked on two wires. Drip zone 2. The drip line runs along the north edge. The west end sits low and is slow to dry after rain.
Bed 4: zucchini, Dunja. Drip zone 2. Garlic goes in here in October 2026 for 2027.
Bed 5: bush beans, Provider. Drip zone 3.
Bed 6: garlic, Music, planted October 2025. Buckwheat cover after the harvest. Drip zone 3.

Drip zone valves are at the east header by the well. Zone 2 shares a header with the greenhouse line.

2026-07-02. Bed 3 (tomato). Kocide 3000 (copper hydroxide). Rate 1.75 g/L. 60 L. Target: early blight, preventive before a wet week; no symptoms yet. Applicator: Maria Lopez.

2026-07-10. Bed 3 (tomato). Kocide 3000 (copper hydroxide). Rate 1.75 g/L. 60 L. Target: early blight, rings on the lower leaves at the west end. Applicator: Dev Patel.

2026-07-17. Bed 3 (tomato). Kocide 3000 (copper hydroxide). Rate 1.75 g/L. 60 L. Target: early blight. Applicator: Dev Patel.

2026-07-24. Bed 3 (tomato). Kocide 3000 (copper hydroxide). Rate 1.75 g/L. 60 L. Target: early blight. Applicator: Sam Okafor.

2026-08-06. Bed 4 (zucchini). Microthiol Disperss (sulfur). Rate 3 g/L. 30 L. Target: powdery mildew. Sprayed before 9am, 21 C. Applicator: Sam Okafor.

2026-08-20. Bed 4 (zucchini). Microthiol Disperss (sulfur). Rate 3 g/L. 30 L. Target: powdery mildew. Applicator: Sam Okafor.

2026-08-28. Bed 3 (tomato). Kocide 3000 (copper hydroxide). Rate 1.75 g/L. 60 L. Target: early blight, rings back on the upper leaves at the east end. Applicator: Maria Lopez.

2026-09-04. Bed 3 (tomato). Kocide 3000 (copper hydroxide). Rate 1.75 g/L. 60 L. Target: early blight. Sixth copper application on bed 3 this season, the SOP limit. Applicator: Dev Patel.

No applications on beds 1, 5 or 6 in 2026.

chat.question: What has the crew reported about bed 3 in #field-reports?
chat.text:
The crew has been posting about bed 3 in #field-reports all season. One report clashes with this scan, so here it is first.

On 1 October, Dev wrote: "Tomato plants out of bed 3. Bagged the diseased ones for the landfill, not the compost." But this scan of a tomato in bed 3 is from 24 October. So either some plants were left in, there are volunteers, or the scan was linked to the wrong bed. Can you check which it is? If the bed really is empty, most of the current plan doesn't apply anymore.

Here is the rest of the history, in order:
- **8 May (Sam):** compost spread on beds 3, 4 and 5.
- **26 June (Dev):** tomatoes tied to the second wire. Lower leaves pruned for airflow.
- **9 July (Dev):** brown spots with target rings and yellow around them on the lower leaves. About 8 plants at the west end were affected. Dev thought it looked like early blight. Maria said to bag the worst leaves, not compost them, and spray copper the next day. Dev filled two bags.
- **14 July (Sam):** lower leaves looked stable after the copper, with no new spots.
- **17 and 24 July (Dev, Sam):** more copper sprays, both logged.
- **28 July (June):** first ripe tomatoes. By 8 August, June reported a good weekly harvest in #crew.
- **27 August (Sam):** the rings came back after heavy rain, this time on upper leaves and a few stems at the east end. Maria called for copper the next morning and for bagging the infected leaves.
- **18 September (Dev):** the blight hadn't spread past the east end, and the fruit was still clean.

The Spray log 2026 matches these reports. It lists six copper hydroxide sprays on bed 3 against early blight between 2 July and 4 September. The 4 September entry is marked as the farm's season limit.

The crew always called it early blight, with target rings. This scan points to Septoria leaf spot instead: small round spots with pale centres and tiny black specks. The early blight score in this scan was much lower. If you're not sure which it is, a sharp close-up of a spotted leaf would help, or you can ask your local extension office. Either way, the clean-up steps are much the same for both diseases.
